deep.reconstruction:
The page contains no mathematical derivations. It is a philosophical text from Riemann's 'Naturphilosophie' fragments on causality, the material published by Weber/Dedekind among the 'Fragmente philosophischen Inhalts' in the Gesammelte Werke (1876, 2nd ed. 1892). It has three parts.

(1) Left column, top, thesis IV (it continues the numbered theses I-III on the previous folio). An action of an agent that is a state or relation (Zustand/Verhältnis) can only act on things capable of the same state or relation. On which of these things it acts, and whether it acts at all, cannot be inferred from the concept of the agent alone.

(2) Remark on Kant. Kant was right that analysing the concept of a thing shows neither that it exists nor that it causes something else. Existence and causality are therefore not analytic marks of a concept and can only be taken from experience. But Kant later grounds the causal concept in an a priori constitution of the knowing subject and reduces it to a mere rule of temporal succession. On that view any perception could in principle be linked as cause with any other as effect. Riemann calls this 'throwing out the baby with the bathwater'. His point: causal relations must indeed come from experience, but we should not give up correcting and completing our grasp of these facts by reflection.

(3) After a marked gap ('Lücke'), a terminological note. German renders both actio and effectus as 'Wirkung'. Since the effectus sense is far more common, using 'Wirkung' for actio is ambiguous. His examples are the usual translations of 'actio aequalis est reactioni' (Newton's third law) and 'principium actionis minimae' (Maupertuis' least-action principle). This continues on the next folio with Kant's habit of adding 'actio' in parentheses.

Right column: this completes the sentence 'Ihr Ergebniss besteht darin,' from the previous page. The result of the preceding considerations is to keep the principle 'what an agent strives to bring about must be determined by the concept of the agent'. That principle should not be applied, as Leibniz or Spinoza did, to substances (Wesen) with a manifold of determinations. It should be applied to real grounds (Realgründe) of the greatest possible simplicity.

A later pencil note reads 'S. 10!', apparently an editorial cross-reference.

There is no computation. The page's only link to mathematics is its context: the next folio begins 'Molecularmechanik' with Gauss's principle of least constraint.
errors: No mathematical content, so there are no mathematical errors to check.

One philosophical point is contestable: Kant's Second Analogy does not make causality an arbitrary rule linking any perception with any other. It makes it a necessary rule of temporal order. Riemann's paraphrase is polemical and somewhat uncharitable, though it reflects the common Herbartian-style criticism.

results.what: Critique of Kant's a priori account of causality: causal relations are empirical, but our grasp of them should be corrected by reflection; the agent principle applies to maximally simple real grounds rather than to Leibnizian/Spinozist substances.
results.usually_credited_to: Background: Hume, Kant (Critique of Pure Reason, 1781/87), Herbart

results.what: Terminological remark that German 'Wirkung' conflates actio and effectus, as in 'actio = reactio' and the 'principium actionis minimae'.
results.modern_name: Terminology of Newton's third law and Maupertuis' least-action principle

deep.surprise_reason: This is purely philosophical text from Riemann's Naturphilosophie fragments, which were published in his Gesammelte Werke. It contains no mathematics and nothing unknown.
transcription_corrections: The thesis number at the top left appears in the image as 'IV.' (continuing I-III on the previous folio), not 'II.'.
'reactio ni' is split across a line break in the manuscript; read 'actio aequalis est reactioni'.

The interlinear insertion reads 'Sein und Causalität kein analytisches Merkmal sei', added above the struck-through 'Seins und der Causalität nicht analytisch sein'. The transcription is consistent with the image here.
'S. 10!' is a later pencil annotation in a different hand, not part of Riemann's text.
